idiom_name: Celery task_routes (dict, glob, regex, or a router class) plus kombu Queue(routing_key)/Exchange(type='topic')
implementation_notes: Celery implements the router as configuration: task_routes maps task names to routing options such as {'queue': 'feed_tasks', 'routing_key': 'feed.import'}, accepts exact names, glob patterns and compiled regexes, and also accepts a router class or function whose route_for_task/route returns the same dict - so the decision can be data or code without changing the pattern. Underneath, kombu Queue(routing_key=...) with Exchange(..., type='topic') lets the broker evaluate the key, which is the real content-based routing; on non-AMQP transports (Redis, SQS) the exchange is emulated by using the queue name, so those semantics degrade. Hand-write a dispatcher (dict of asyncio.Queue keyed by header) only for in-process flows where a task queue would be a needless dependency.
code_sketch:
from kombu import Queue
import re

app.conf.task_default_exchange_type = 'topic'
app.conf.task_queues = (Queue('feed_tasks', routing_key='feed.#'),)
app.conf.task_routes = ([
    ('feed.tasks.*', {'queue': 'feed_tasks', 'routing_key': 'feed.import'}),
    (re.compile(r'(video|image)\.tasks\..*'), {'queue': 'media'}),
],)  # ordered items: first match wins
pitfalls: A route that matches nothing is not an error: the task falls back to task_default_queue, so a typo in a glob silently sends work to the default worker.
The dict form of task_routes has no precedence guarantee; if rule order matters the items-list form (list of pairs inside a tuple) must be used.
Routing is applied at publish time while workers consume whatever their -Q list declares, so a routing change also requires redeploying the worker queues.
Non-AMQP transports ignore exchange and routing-key semantics, so a topic-routing design silently degrades to queue-name routing on Redis or SQS.
